content: Calcium hypochlorite is a chemical compound with the formula Ca(OCl)₂. It is commonly used for water treatment and as a bleaching agent, often referred to as bleaching powder. This compound is relatively stable and contains a higher available chlorine content compared to sodium hypochlorite (liquid bleach). Preparation Calcium hypochlorite is produced through either the calcium process or the sodium process. Bleaching powder is essentially a mixture of calcium hypochlorite (Ca(OCl)₂), basic calcium chloride (CaCl₂), calcium hydroxide (Ca(OH)₂), and water, along with some slaked lime (Ca(OH)₂). Properties Calcium hypochlorite appears as a yellowish-white solid with a strong chlorine odor. It has limited solubility in water, making it more suitable for use in soft to moderately hard water. It is available in two forms: a dry form and a hydrated form, with the latter being safer to handle. When calcium hypochlorite reacts with carbon dioxide, it forms calcium carbonate and releases chlorine gas. Similarly, it reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce calcium chloride. Extreme caution is required when handling this compound. It should be stored in a cool, dry place, away from organic materials. When mixing with water, it is safest to add the calcium hypochlorite to the water, not the other way around. This material is known to undergo self-heating and rapid decomposition, which can release toxic chlorine gas. Uses Calcium hypochlorite is widely used for disinfecting drinking water and swimming pool water. In outdoor swimming pools, it can be used as a sanitizer in combination with a cyanuric acid stabilizer, which helps reduce chlorine loss due to UV radiation. However, calcium in the compound can contribute to water hardness and may clog filters. Some formulations of calcium hypochlorite include anti-scaling agents to prevent clogging in pipes and filters, making them suitable for use in hard water. One of the main advantages of calcium hypochlorite is that it is unstabilized, unlike chlorinated isocyanurates such as sodium dichloroisocyanurate or trichloroisocyanuric acid, which contain cyanuric acid. Excessive cyanuric acid levels can impair chlorine's effectiveness. Pools using chlorinated isocyanurates should maintain a free chlorine level of 2–5 ppm, whereas pools using calcium hypochlorite should maintain a chlorine level of 1–2 ppm. In addition to its use in water treatment, calcium hypochlorite (commonly known as bleaching powder) is also employed for bleaching cotton and linen and in the production of chloroform.
